blocks.text: For just as prudence without simplicity degenerates into cunning, so simplicity without prudence is nothing but foolishness and stupidity. The prudent in Hebrew are ערומים, and the simple פתיים, or פתאים. Solomon often sets these two against each other. Thus Prov. I, 4. לתת לפתאים ערמה, to give prudence to the simple. Prov. VIII, 5. O ye simple, understand prudence. Prov. XIV, 15. פתי, the simple believes every word, וערום, but the prudent considers his step. Prov. XIX, 25. ופתי יערים, And the simple will become prudent. Prov. XXII, 3. ערום, The prudent, when he sees evil, hides himself, ופתיים, but the simple pass on and are punished. And, [col. 20] just as the serpent is called ערום, φρόνιμος [phronimos], Gen. III, 1., so the dove is called פתה, simple, Os. VII, 11. And Ephraim has become כיונה פתה אין לב, like a simple dove, lacking heart, that is, senseless. To these two passages Christ no doubt alluded. You may object that both are put as vices: that the serpent is called ערום not because it is prudent but because it is crafty and wily, and the dove פתה not because it is simple but because it is foolish, and אין לב, senseless, as immediately follows. I reply, first, that both [II, 550] ערום and פתי or פתה are neutral words, which according to their subject may also turn to praise. Thus ערום means not only crafty and cunning but also prudent, and ערמה prudence, as the passages of Solomon cited above amply show. Conversely פתי signifies not only ἄφρονα [aphrona], foolish, but also ἀκέραιον [akeraion], simple, as in Ps. CXVI, 6. שמר פתאים יהוה, the Lord preserves the simple. Christ could therefore use these words in praise as well. Second, neither the serpent's prudence nor the dove's simplicity is praised by Christ on its own and torn from the other; they are praised only when joined together, so that the one supplies what is lacking in the other, or corrects what is excessive. In the same way, from two drugs that are harmful separately a third is compounded that is useful and wholesome, because they temper each other. Hence the ancients so often join these two. Gregory of Nazianzus, on his father, Oration 19: Τὸ γὰρ τοῦ ὄφεως φρόνιμον περὶ τὸ κακὸν τῷ τῆς περιστερᾶς ἀκεραίῳ περὶ τὸ καλὸν ἀναμίξας, οὐδὲ τὸ φρόνιμον εἴασε κακοῦργον γενέσθαι. οὔτε τὸ ἁπλοῦν ἀνόητον, ἀλλ᾽ ἓν ἀρετῆς εἶδος, ὡς μάλιστα ἐνῆν, ἐξ ἀμφοτέρων ἀπηκριβώσατο. [To gar tou opheōs phronimon peri to kakon tō tēs peristeras akeraiō peri to kalon anamixas, oude to phronimon eiase kakourgon genesthai. oute to haploun anoēton, all᾽ hen aretēs eidos, hōs malista enēn, ex amphoterōn apēkribōsato.] Having joined the serpent's prudence regarding evil with the dove's simplicity regarding good, he so conducted himself that he let neither prudence degenerate into cunning wickedness nor simplicity into stupidity, but from both, as far as was possible, he produced a single form of virtue, perfect and complete in every respect. Jerome, to Paulinus on the training of a monk: Have the simplicity of the dove, so as not to contrive snares against anyone, and the cunning of the serpent, so as not to be tripped up by the plots of others. Isidore of Pelusium, book 3, epist. 175: Ἡ φρόνησις τῇ ἁπλότητι κιρνωμένη θεῖόν τι χρῆμα· φημὶ δὲ ἐντελεστάτην ἀρετὴν ἀποτελεῖ· εἰ δὲ θατέρα θατέρας χωρισθείη, ἡ μὲν εἰς πονηρίαν ἐμπίπτει, ἡ δὲ εἰς μωρίαν τελευτᾷ· [Hē phronēsis tē haplotēti kirnōmenē theion ti chrēma; phēmi de entelestatēn aretēn apotelei; ei de thatera thateras chōristheiē, hē men eis ponērian empiptei, hē de eis mōrian teleuta;] Prudence tempered with simplicity produces something divine, that is, a virtue complete in every respect. But if the one is separated from the other, the former falls into perversity, while the latter ends in folly. Faustus, On Free Will, book 2, last chapter: Let us make man simple, let us make him astute: simple, so that being crafty he may not inflict evil; astute, so that being incautious he may not fall into it. Gregory on Job, book 1, ch. 2: He necessarily joined both in the admonition, so that the cunning of the serpent might equip the simplicity of the dove, and in turn the simplicity of the dove might temper the cunning of the serpent. Sidonius, book 7, Epist. 13, on Lupus, bishop of Troyes: In the church he keeps the simplicity of the dove, in the forum the cunning of the serpent. To the good he is judged prudent, to the wicked wary, to neither crafty. St Bernard, Epist. 327, to Pope Innocent: in the church, then, simplicity must be kept, in the forum cunning; here, lest you be deceived, there, lest you deceive. See more on this subject in Caesarius, Dial. 4, Quaest. 190. Further, the simple are here called not ἁπλοί [haploi] but ἀκέραιοι [akeraioi]. Yet it comes to the same thing. For ἀκέραιος [akeraios], formed from κεράω [keraō], misceo [I mix], properly signifies that which has nothing external and foreign mixed into it. Some take ἀκέραιος [akeraios] to be the same as ἀκερᾶς [akeras] or ἀκέρατος [akeratos], [II, 551] that which has no horns, and hence is ἀβλαβής [ablabēs] and harmless, a metaphor taken from animals that strike with the horn. So the Arabic and Ethiopic translators seem to have taken it: in the former ἀκέραιοι [akeraioi] are ودعا [wudaʿā], in the latter የዋሃን፡, that is, mild and gentle. But the first etymology seems more regular. Nor is it quite fitting that hornless should be said for harmless, since eagles, lions and many other wild beasts [col. 21] that have no horns possess many ways of doing harm, which they employ to destroy other animals. Moreover, the simple are opposed to the prudent, but the mild and gentle are not. So if you render mild, the grace of the opposition will be lost, which is evident here between the serpent's prudence and the dove's simplicity. Of the same kind is that of Paul, Rom. XVI, 19: I would have you σοφούς [sophous] wise in what is good, ἀκεραίους δέ [akeraious de], but simple in what is evil. The illustrious Beza had rendered innocent in his first editions, but in later ones he rightly changed it to simple, so that the opposition might stand ^{(1)}. To the same effect is the fact that in that very ancient manuscript of Beza ἁπλούστατοι [haploustatoi], most simple, was read for ἀκέραιοι [akeraioi]. Nor is it a slight point that, just as the serpent's being called prudent is taken from Moses, so the dove's being called simple is taken from Hosea. But no passage of the Prophets occurs where it is called mild. Thus the Christian Arabs seem to have understood less well what ἀκέραιοι [akeraioi] means here than the Muslim doctors, who render بلها [bulhan] bulhan, that is, simple. So in the book of the priest Achmed entitled الزهد [al-zuhd], that is, abstinence, Iazid, son of Malzara, says that Jesus commanded his disciples ان يكون بلها في الله مشل الحمام [an yakūna bulhan fī Allāh mashl al-ḥamām] that they should be bulhan (that is, simple) in God like doves. Thus we render بلها [bulhan] bulhan, with the most learned of the Arabs, from the singular ابله [ablah] ablaho, to which كيس [kayyis] chaison is opposed, that is, cunning and crafty. And that it is to be so taken is shown by what follows in the same place: ليس شي ابله من الحمام وذلك انك تاخذ فرخيه من تحته فتذبحهما ثم يعود الي مكانه فيفرخ فيه [laysa shay ablah min al-ḥamām wa-dhālika annaka taʾkhudh farkhayhi min taḥtihi fa-tadhbaḥuhumā thumma yaʿūd ilā makānihi fa-yufarrikh fīhi] Nothing is simpler than the dove. For even if you kill the young taken from under it, it nevertheless soon returns to its place and hatches young in it. The very same thing the Fathers write on the passage of Hosea we have cited. Theodoret: Ἐκείνη τῶν ἰδίων νεοττῶν ἀφαιρουμένη οὐκ ἀφίπταται, ἀλλὰ τοῖς αὐτοῖς προστρέχει χωρίοις. [Ekeinē tōn idiōn neottōn aphairoumenē ouk aphiptatai, alla tois autois prostrechei chōriois.] And following him Theophylact: When its young are taken away it does not fly off, but remains in the same places. Somewhat differently Jerome: Other birds hasten to protect their young even at the risk of their own life, and when they see a hawk, a snake, a raven or a crow approach their nest, [II, 552] they flutter this way and that, throw themselves at it, tear it with beak and claws, and bear witness to a parent's grief with plaintive cry. The dove alone does not grieve for its young when they are taken away, nor seek them. But how truly, I do not quite know, since a kind of dove or wood-pigeon, الورشان [al-warashān] alvvarsen, is described by the Arabs بالحنو علي اولاده حتي انه ربما قتل نفسه اذا راها في يد القانص [bi-l-ḥunuww ʿalā awlādihi ḥattā annahu rubbamā qatala nafsahu idhā rāhā fī yad al-qāniṣ] as burning with such affection for its young that it sometimes kills itself when it sees them in the fowler's hand. So it is found in Damir. And in general writers commend the dove for its love of its offspring. Pliny, book 10, ch. 34, on the male and female dove: Both have equal love for their offspring; often for this reason there is chastisement, when the female is slow in going in to the young. On which more in Aristotle, Hist. book 9, ch. 7; Aelian, Hist. book 3, ch. 45; again Aelian, Var. book 1, ch. 15; Athenaeus, book 9, ch. 11; Porphyry, Περὶ ἀποχῆς [Peri apochēs], etc., book 3; which there is no room to copy out here. Others assert that the dove's simplicity is evident in the fact that it does not avoid nets, nor the snares laid for it, [col. 22] when it comes down to feed. And with this stupidity of the dove they would have Hosea compare the sloth of the Israelites, who took no precaution against dangers and threw themselves into the power of their enemies. However that may be, this simplicity of the dove was recognized also by οἱ ἔξωθεν [hoi exōthen]. Thus on that line of Juvenal,
